positions/christian-zionism/oneLine: Christians should support the return of the Jewish people to the land of Israel and, for many adherents, the modern State of Israel, as the fulfilment of biblical promise and prophecy.
positions/christian-zionism/coreClaims/0: God’s covenant with Abraham, including the land, remains in force for the Jewish people (Gen 12:3; 17:8).
positions/christian-zionism/coreClaims/1: The modern return of Jews to the land and the founding of Israel (1948) fulfil prophecy (Ezek 36–37; Amos 9:14–15).
positions/christian-zionism/coreClaims/2: Those who bless Abraham’s descendants will be blessed (Gen 12:3), so Christians have a duty to support Israel.
positions/christian-zionism/coreClaims/3: In dispensational forms, Israel’s restoration is a key sign of the approaching end times.
positions/christian-zionism/origin: Puritan "restorationists" (Thomas Brightman, 1615; Increase Mather) expected a return of the Jews before their conversion. In 19th-century Britain, Lord Shaftesbury and others promoted Jewish settlement; dispensationalists (Darby, Blackstone, whose 1891 Memorial petitioned President Harrison) made restoration central. Arthur Balfour and Lloyd George, raised in evangelical homes, issued the Balfour Declaration (1917). After 1948 and especially 1967 it became a mass movement among American evangelicals (International Christian Embassy Jerusalem 1980; Christians United for Israel 2006).
positions/christian-zionism/proponentsOt: Many African, Latin American and Korean Pentecostals
positions/christian-zionism/strongestArg: Paul insists that God has not rejected his people Israel and that "the gifts and calling of God are without repentance" (Rom 11:1, 29), which arguably includes the land.
Centuries of Christian anti-Judaism and supersessionism contributed to the Holocaust; affirming Israel’s ongoing election is a needed correction.
The survival of the Jewish people and their return to the land after nearly 1,900 years is, to many, a historically remarkable event that invites theological interpretation.
positions/christian-zionism/strongestObj: Palestinian Christians (Naim Ateek, Sabeel; Kairos Palestine 2009), Middle Eastern church leaders (Jerusalem Declaration on Christian Zionism, 2006) and many Catholic, Orthodox and mainline bodies argue it ignores justice for Palestinians, including fellow Christians.
Covenant and Reformed theologians argue that the New Testament universalises the land promise to "the world" (Rom 4:13) and fulfils it in Christ and the new creation (Heb 11:16).
Critics charge it instrumentalises Jews within an end-times script (often including a future mass conversion or tribulation), which some Jewish observers find troubling.
It can fuse prophecy with partisan foreign policy, discouraging peace efforts thought to delay prophetic fulfilment.
positions/christian-zionism/responses/0: Christian Zionists reply that supporting Israel’s existence is compatible with concern for Palestinians, and many fund Arab Christian ministries.
positions/christian-zionism/responses/1: Non-dispensational Christian Zionists (McDermott and others) ground their view in covenant faithfulness and repentance for anti-Judaism rather than in end-time timetables.
positions/christian-zionism/responses/2: They argue that denying Jewish people a place in God’s continuing purposes risks repeating historic Christian contempt for Judaism.
positions/christian-zionism/consequences: Contributed to British support for a Jewish homeland (Balfour Declaration, 1917).
Made evangelicals one of the strongest US constituencies for the State of Israel, influencing foreign policy (e.g. the 2018 US embassy move to Jerusalem was widely welcomed by Christian Zionists).
Created sharp tensions between Western evangelicals and Middle Eastern churches.
Spurred Christian–Jewish dialogue as well as controversy within Jewish communities about evangelical support.
positions/realized-eschatology/oneLine: The kingdom of God and the "last things" have essentially arrived in the ministry, death and resurrection of Jesus; eschatology is about present encounter rather than future events.
positions/realized-eschatology/coreClaim: Jesus proclaimed the kingdom as already present: "the kingdom of God is come upon you" (Matt 12:28).
Judgement and eternal life are present realities for those who believe (John 3:18; 5:24).
Apocalyptic future language in the New Testament is largely a later development or a mythological way of expressing the significance of the present moment of decision.
The Church lives in the age of fulfilment.
positions/realized-eschatology/origin: Coined by C. H. Dodd (The Parables of the Kingdom, 1935) in reaction to Johannes Weiss and Albert Schweitzer’s "consistent" (thoroughgoing) eschatology (1892; The Quest of the Historical Jesus, 1906), which argued Jesus mistakenly expected an imminent cosmic end. Related to Rudolf Bultmann’s existential "demythologising" of New Testament eschatology (1941) and to Johannine "realized" emphases noticed by many patristic writers.
positions/realized-eschatology/proponent: J. A. T. Robinson (Jesus and His Coming, 1957)
positions/realized-eschatology/strongest: Several sayings of Jesus clearly speak of the kingdom as present in his exorcisms and teaching.
John’s Gospel consistently presents eternal life and judgement as present realities.
It avoids attributing a failed prediction to Jesus, as Schweitzer did.
It cannot account for the many future-oriented sayings (Mark 13; 14:25, 62; "thy kingdom come") without excising them as inauthentic.
Dodd himself later moved toward an "inaugurated" view (he endorsed the phrase "eschatology in process of realization").
Critics argue it reduces Christian hope to present experience, abandoning bodily resurrection and new creation affirmed by the creeds.
positions/realized-eschatology/responses: Proponents reply that future images are symbolic expressions of the ultimate significance of God’s present act in Christ.
Some argue that the living encounter with God in Christ is itself the deepest content of resurrection hope, and that this is how John intends it.
positions/realized-eschatology/consequen: Shifted 20th-century New Testament scholarship away from Schweitzer’s "failed apocalyptic prophet" picture.
Helped produce the "already/not yet" synthesis of inaugurated eschatology.
Influenced liberal and existentialist preaching that de-emphasised literal future events.
positions/inaugurated-eschatology/oneLin: The kingdom of God has truly begun in Jesus’ ministry, death, resurrection and the gift of the Spirit, but will only be consummated at his return; the Church lives "between the times".
positions/inaugurated-eschatology/coreCl: The age to come has broken into this present age in Jesus without yet ending it; the two ages overlap.
The resurrection of Jesus is the "firstfruits" of the general resurrection (1 Cor 15:20–23), and the Spirit is the "down payment" of the inheritance (Eph 1:14).
Christ will return bodily to complete the kingdom, raise the dead and renew creation.
Christian ethics and mission are signs of the coming kingdom within present history.
positions/inaugurated-eschatology/origin: Anticipated by Geerhardus Vos’ two-age schema (The Pauline Eschatology, 1930), developed by Oscar Cullmann (Christ and Time, 1946, with the analogy of D-Day and V-Day), Joachim Jeremias, W. G. Kümmel and Herman Ridderbos, and popularised among evangelicals by George Eldon Ladd. Jürgen Moltmann’s Theology of Hope (1964) and N. T. Wright’s new-creation eschatology are influential variants.
positions/inaugurated-eschatology/propon: Many Catholic and Orthodox theologians (Eucharist as foretaste of the eschaton)
positions/inaugurated-eschatology/strong: It integrates both sets of Jesus’ sayings (kingdom present and kingdom future) without dismissing either.
It matches Paul’s two-age framework, in which believers already have the Spirit but "groan" awaiting the redemption of the body (Rom 8:23).
It commands broad support across Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant and Pentecostal scholarship, and is compatible with several millennial views.
It grounds both present social engagement and future hope, avoiding both escapism and utopianism.
Critics say "already/not yet" can become a formula that explains away tensions rather than resolving them.
It does not settle the millennial question; amillennialists, premillennialists and postmillennialists all claim it.
Some (Moltmann, liberation theologians) are accused of politicising the "not yet"; others of so stressing the "already" that they fall into triumphalism (e.g. over-realized healing claims).
positions/inaugurated-eschatology/respon: Proponents answer that the tension is not a theological convenience but the actual shape of the New Testament witness, which is christologically centred.
They acknowledge it is a framework, not a full map, and that its strength lies precisely in being shared across millennial positions.
positions/inaugurated-eschatology/conseq: Became the broad consensus framework of 20th-century biblical scholarship.
Informs the Lausanne Movement’s and Catholic social teaching’s integration of evangelism and social action as kingdom signs.
Shaped Pentecostal theology of healing as a foretaste, and Orthodox and Catholic liturgical theology of the Eucharist as anticipation of the heavenly banquet.
positions/just-war/oneLine: War is always tragic, but legitimate authorities may use proportionate force as a last resort to defend the innocent and restore a just peace, under strict moral limits.
positions/just-war/coreClaims/0: Love of neighbour can require protecting the innocent from aggression, including by force.
positions/just-war/coreClaims/1: Jus ad bellum: legitimate authority, just cause, right intention, last resort, reasonable hope of success, proportionality.
positions/just-war/coreClaims/2: Jus in bello: discrimination (non-combatants may not be directly targeted) and proportionality in means.
positions/just-war/coreClaims/3: The ruler bears the sword as God’s servant (Rom 13:4); private vengeance remains forbidden.
positions/just-war/coreClaims/4: The goal of war is peace (Augustine, City of God 19.12).
positions/just-war/keyTexts/3: Augustine, Reply to Faustus 22.74–75; City of God 19
positions/just-war/origin: Drawing on Cicero and Ambrose (On the Duties of the Clergy, c.391), Augustine (c.400–420) gave Christian shape to a theory of justified war; Gratian’s Decretum (c.1140) and Thomas Aquinas (c.1272) systematised it; Francisco de Vitoria (1539), Francisco Suárez and Hugo Grotius (On the Law of War and Peace, 1625) developed it into international law. Affirmed by Lutheran (Augsburg XVI), Anglican (Article XXXVII) and Reformed confessions and the Catholic Catechism (§2307–2317); revived in the 20th century by Reinhold Niebuhr, Paul Ramsey and the US Catholic bishops’ The Challenge of Peace (1983).
positions/just-war/strongestArguments/0: Refusing to defend the innocent against aggression can itself be a failure of love; the Good Samaritan would not have stood by during the assault.
positions/just-war/strongestArguments/1: Scripture never requires soldiers to leave the army (Luke 3:14; Acts 10) and affirms the ruler’s sword (Rom 13:4).
positions/just-war/strongestArguments/2: It restrains war rather than glorifying it, and its criteria shaped the Geneva Conventions and international humanitarian law.
positions/just-war/strongestArguments/3: It has been the mainstream position of most churches for 1,600 years.
positions/just-war/strongestObjections/0: Pacifists argue that Jesus’ explicit teaching ("love your enemies", "put up again thy sword") and the pre-Constantinian Church’s practice exclude killing.
positions/just-war/strongestObjections/1: In practice the criteria have been bent to bless almost every war, including crusades and conquests, and rarely stop a government from fighting.
positions/just-war/strongestObjections/2: Modern total war and weapons of mass destruction make discrimination and proportionality nearly impossible; Pope Francis (Fratelli Tutti §258, 2020) doubted that just-war criteria can still be met.
positions/just-war/strongestObjections/3: Eastern Orthodoxy never developed a formal just-war theory, treating killing even in war as requiring repentance (Basil, canon 13).
positions/just-war/responses/0: Just-war thinkers reply that abuse of the criteria condemns the abusers, not the criteria, and that the tradition has produced real limits on warfare.
positions/just-war/responses/1: They argue that Jesus’ teaching concerns personal retaliation, while Romans 13 addresses the public office of protecting others.
positions/just-war/responses/2: Many accept a "presumption against war" (Challenge of Peace, 1983), narrowing the tradition towards pacifism in practice.
positions/just-war/consequences/0: Became the moral framework of Western Christendom and of modern international law.
positions/just-war/consequences/1: Enabled Christian participation in states, armies and politics.
positions/just-war/consequences/2: Used critically to oppose specific wars (e.g. Vietnam, Iraq 2003) and to condemn nuclear deterrence policies.
